extracted.intended_audience: Parties and counsel participating in AIA trial proceedings before the PTAB (petitioners, patent owners, and their lawyers)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical and procedural guidance for conducting AIA trial proceedings (IPR, PGR, CBM, derivation) before the Patent Trial and Appeal Board, including expert testimony, petitions and motions practice, institution considerations, evidentiary challenges, oral hearings, and a sample scheduling order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expert witness qualification (Fed. R. Evid. 702)
rubrics_metrics.description: An expert witness must be qualified as an expert by knowledge, skill, experience, training, or education to testify in the form of an opinion. There is no requirement of a perfect match between the expert’s experience and the relevant field; a person need not be a person of ordinary skill in the art but must be 'qualified in the pertinent art.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples/citations: SEB S.A. v. Montgomery Ward & Co., Sundance, Inc. v. DeMonte Fabricating. Absence of an advanced degree does not preclude testimony if experience supplies sufficient qualification. Qualification is judged under Fed. R. Evid. 702.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form and uses of expert testimony
rubrics_metrics.description: Expert testimony is presented in the form of an affidavit or declaration (37 C.F.R. § 42.53(a)). Experts may explain the relevant technology, establish the level of skill in the art, describe the person of ordinary skill, testify about teachings of prior art and their relation to patentability, opine on reasons to combine references or expectation of success, and explain objective indicia of nonobviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical uses identified: explaining prior art 'as viewed with the knowledge of one of skill in the art'; explaining objective evidence and how it should be weighed. But testimony must be properly supported (see related criteria on sufficiency and reliability).

rubrics_metrics.name: Required factual support and reliability for expert testimony
rubrics_metrics.description: Expert testimony must be based on sufficient facts and data (Fed. R. Evid. 702(b)), must disclose underlying facts or data (37 C.F.R. § 42.65(a)), must be the product of reliable principles and methods (Fed. R. Evid. 702(c)), and must reliably apply those principles and methods to the facts (Fed. R. Evid. 702(d)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expert testimony that does not disclose the underlying facts or data is entitled to little or no weight. The Board has broad discretion to assign weight to expert testimony (Yorkey v. Diab).

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on reliance upon expert testimony for disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Expert testimony cannot take the place of disclosure in a prior art reference when that disclosure is required (e.g., anticipation requires each claim element expressly or inherently described in a single prior art reference).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples/citations: Verdegaal Bros. v. Union Oil; K/S Himpp v. Hear-Wear. Conclusory third-party assertions without supporting evidence cannot supply a missing limitation. Expert testimony may explain patents/printed publications but cannot substitute for patents/printed publications (35 U.S.C. § 311(b)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Presentation and incorporation limits for expert testimony in filings
rubrics_metrics.description: Parties that incorporate expert testimony by reference in petitions, motions, or replies without providing explanation risk having the testimony not considered by the Board. 37 C.F.R. § 42.6(a)(3) prohibits incorporation by reference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See Cisco Systems v. C-Cation Techs. (informative). Parties should include necessary explanation and not rely on mere incorporation by reference due to word/page limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Word count and page limits (37 C.F.R. § 42.24)
rubrics_metrics.description: A word count limit applies to petitions, patent owner preliminary responses, patent owner responses, and petitioner replies to patent owner responses and any sur-replies; a page limit applies to all other briefing. Limits: 14,000 words for petitions requesting IPR and derivation; 18,700 words for petitions requesting PGR and CBM; motions other than motions to amend limited to 15 pages; motions to amend limited to 25 pages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patent owner preliminary responses and patent owner responses are subject to same word limits as corresponding petition. Replies to patent owner responses limited to 5,600 words. Replies to oppositions to motions to amend limited to 12 pages; replies to other oppositions limited to 5 pages. Sur-replies, if authorized, are subject to same word/page limits as the reply unless ordered otherwise. Parties must include a certification stating the number of words (§ 42.24(d)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Word-count certification and exclusions
rubrics_metrics.description: Any paper constrained by type-volume limits must include a certification stating the number of words, and a party may rely on their word-processing system's word count.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exempt from word count: table of contents, table of authorities, mandatory notices under § 42.8, certificate of service, or appendix of exhibits or claim listing; but this exemption does not apply to grounds for standing. Parties need not include a statement of material facts; double spacing is not required for claim charts (§ 42.6(a)(2)(iii)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on abusing word-count limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Parties should not abuse the word-count limits by using excessive words in figures/drawings/images, deleting spacing between words, or using excessive acronyms/abbreviations to circumvent the rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Board will generally accept a party’s certification absent obvious abuse. Examples/citations: Pi-Net Int’l, Inc. v. JPMorgan Chase & Co. If a party feels prejudice from an alleged violation, raise the issue promptly and try to remedy before approaching the Board; the Board will consider violations case-by-case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concise presentation and issue selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective writing is concise writing; parties should avoid submitting a repository of all possible information and should focus on concise, well-organized, easy-to-follow arguments supported by readily identifiable evidence of record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presentation of too many issues tends to detract from arguments and may cause meritorious issues to be missed or discounted. Extended discussions of general patent law principles may be unnecessary unless the law is disputed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory institution standard and Director's discretion (35 U.S.C. §§ 314(a), 324(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board institutes trial on behalf of the Director and in deciding whether to institute considers at minimum whether a party has satisfied the relevant statutory institution standard. Sections 314(a) and 324(a) provide the Director with discretion to deny a petition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Once instituted, petitioner is entitled to a final written decision addressing all claims challenged (SAS Institute v. Iancu). Director's discretion is informed by statutory obligations (35 U.S.C. § 316(a)(2), § 316(b) and § 326(b)) to consider economy, integrity of patent system, efficient administration, and timeliness.

rubrics_metrics.name: General Plastic non-exhaustive factors for follow-on petitions
rubrics_metrics.description: When exercising discretion on instituting IPR for follow-on petitions, the Board considers non-exclusive factors including: (1) whether same petitioner previously filed on same claims; (2) whether petitioner knew or should have known of prior art asserted in second petition at time of first petition; (3) whether petitioner had preliminary response or institution decision on first petition when filing second; (4) elapsed time between learning of prior art and filing second petition; (5) whether petitioner provides adequate explanation for time elapsed; (6) finite resources of the Board; (7) requirement to issue final determination within one year of institution (35 U.S.C. § 316(a)(11)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The factors are not dispositive, not exclusive, and are part of a balanced assessment including the merits. There is no per se rule precluding follow-on petitions; other circumstances (e.g., related proceedings in district court or ITC) may also inform discretion.

rubrics_metrics.name: 35 U.S.C. § 325(d) considerations and Becton Dickinson non-exhaustive factors
rubrics_metrics.description: In determining whether to order reexamination or institute an IPR/PGR/CBM, the Director may take into account whether the same or substantially the same prior art or arguments were previously presented to the Office. The Board balances petitioner’s desire to be heard against the patent owner’s interest in avoiding duplicative challenges and considers efficient administration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Becton Dickinson factors considered include: (1) similarities and material differences between asserted art and prior art during examination; (2) cumulative nature of asserted art; (3) extent to which asserted art was evaluated during examination; (4) overlap between arguments made during examination and petitioner’s reliance; (5) whether petitioner pointed out how the Office erred in evaluating the art; (6) extent to which additional evidence/facts in the petition warrant reconsideration. Board may consider materially changed circumstances or new evidence not available previously.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope and limits of replies and sur-replies (37 C.F.R. § 42.23)
rubrics_metrics.description: A petitioner may file a reply to a patent owner response; a patent owner may file a reply to an opposition to a motion to amend. Petitioner, in its reply, may address issues discussed in the institution decision; patent owner may address the institution decision in its sur-reply. Generally, replies or sur-replies may only respond to arguments raised in the preceding brief.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Petitioner may not submit new evidence or arguments in reply that it could have presented earlier, but may submit directly responsive rebuttal evidence. New expert declaration in reply permits opposing party to cross-examine and move to exclude. Sur-replies to principal briefs normally authorized by scheduling order; sur-replies may not be accompanied by new evidence other than deposition transcripts of cross-examination. Replies raising new issues or new theories (e.g., new rationale to combine references) may not be considered (Intelligent Bio-Systems v. Illumina). The Board is not required to parse proper from improper portions of replies/sur-replies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing and procedure for challenging admissibility of evidence (motions to exclude)
rubrics_metrics.description: Objections to admissibility must be filed within five business days of service of the evidence objected to, or ten days after institution of trial (37 C.F.R. §§ 42.64(a), 42.64(b)(1)). Supplemental evidence is served (not filed) at time of objection and filed only in support of an opposition to a motion to exclude (§ 42.64(b)(2)). Objections are preserved only by filing a motion to exclude (§ 42.64(c)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Due dates for motion to exclude, opposition, and reply usually set in the Scheduling Order. The Board prefers to wait until after oral hearing to decide motions to exclude but may resolve early via pre-hearing conference for a limited number of objections. Parties may request early resolution where evidence is central and mootness unlikely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Required contents of a motion to exclude
rubrics_metrics.description: A motion to exclude should: (a) identify where in the record the objection originally was made; (b) identify where in the record the evidence sought to be excluded was relied upon by an opponent; (c) address objections to exhibits in numerical order; and (d) explain the basis and grounds for each objection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A motion to exclude must explain why the evidence is not admissible (e.g., relevance or hearsay). It may not be used to challenge sufficiency of the evidence to prove a fact or to argue weight—weight arguments belong in merits documents. Nor should it address arguments exceeding the proper scope of reply or sur-reply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motions to strike and authorization
rubrics_metrics.description: If a party believes an opposing brief raises new issues, belated evidence, or otherwise exceeds proper scope of reply/sur-reply, it may request authorization to file a motion to strike or request further merits briefing (e.g., a sur-reply).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A motion to strike seeks to have the Board disregard arguments/late-filed evidence entirely; further briefing may be preferable to address weight. Striking is an exceptional remedy expected to be granted rarely. Authorization to file a motion to strike should generally be requested within one week of the allegedly improper submission. The Board will decide such requests case-by-case and preferably before oral hearing to avoid wasting hearing time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oral hearing request, time allocation, and pre-hearing conference
rubrics_metrics.description: Each party will have opportunity to present their case before at least three Board members. Request for oral hearing normally set in Scheduling Order; a request should include the amount of time needed. The Board ordinarily provides one hour of argument per side but parties may request more or less. A pre-hearing conference call may be held (generally no later than three business days before hearing) to preview issues and seek guidance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parties are encouraged to confer and jointly agree on argument time and issues for discussion. The pre-hearing conference should preview but not argue issues, identify limited objections for early resolution, and permit discussion on demonstratives or pending motions to strike/exclude. The Board will preferably rule on pending motions during or after the pre-hearing conference but may defer to the hearing or thereafter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oral hearing format and limitations on argument
rubrics_metrics.description: At oral hearing, petitioner generally argues first, followed by patent owner, and petitioner may give a rebuttal (but petitioner may not reserve for rebuttal more than half the total time absent special circumstances). Patent owner may be permitted a brief sur-rebuttal. In multi-party/multi-patent hearings, Board will adopt a fair and efficient format.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parties should jointly propose formats where multiple parties are involved. Board expects parties to preserve efficiency; reserving excessive rebuttal time is limited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstrative exhibits at oral hearing
rubrics_metrics.description: Demonstrative exhibits are aids to oral argument and not evidence; they should be clearly marked 'DEMONSTRATIVE EXHIBIT – NOT EVIDENCE'. Demonstratives should be limited (few slides and handouts/binder); pages should be numbered and exhibit numbers identified during argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstratives cannot advance arguments or introduce evidence not previously presented in the record (Dell Inc. v. Acceleron, LLC). The Board finds elaborate demonstratives more likely to impede than help. Parties are encouraged to exchange and confer on demonstratives to narrow objections; the panel’s order will set procedures for handling objections to demonstratives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Live testimony at oral hearing — when permitted and format
rubrics_metrics.description: Live testimony is permitted when requested by a party and the panel believes it will be helpful; it is considered evidence and normally becomes part of the record. The format is at the panel’s discretion. The Board will consider requests case-by-case and does not expect to permit live testimony in every case with conflicting testimony.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Live testimony more likely allowed where witness demeanor is critical to credibility (e.g., antedating a reference by showing reduction to practice) or where issue is case-dispositive. Live testimony may not exceed the scope of the underlying declaration and may not address new theories or arguments not previously presented.

rubrics_metrics.name: No new evidence or arguments at oral hearing
rubrics_metrics.description: During oral hearing, a party may rely upon demonstratives and evidence previously submitted, but may only present arguments that were relied upon in previously submitted papers; except when live testimony is permitted, no new evidence may be presented at oral argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Live testimony cannot exceed the scope of the underlying declaration and cannot introduce new theories. Untimely arguments raised for the first time at oral argument may be dismissed (Dell Inc. v. Acceleron).

rubrics_metrics.name: Protective orders, sealing, and redactions
rubrics_metrics.description: No protective order applies until the Board enters one. If a motion to seal is filed before entry of a protective order, a jointly proposed protective order must be filed as an exhibit with the motion. The Board encourages adopting the Board’s default protective order; deviations require a marked-up comparison and explanation of good cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board has a strong interest in public availability of trial proceedings. Redactions should be limited to the minimum necessary and the thrust of argument/evidence must remain discernible. Information under protective order may become public if identified in a final written decision; a motion to expunge may not prevail over public interest in a complete file history.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discovery disputes — meet-and-confer requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Parties are encouraged to resolve discovery disputes on their own; they must meet and confer before contacting the Board. If attempts fail, a party may request a conference call with the Board.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a prerequisite before the Board becomes involved in discovery disputes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Testimony Guidelines and sanctions (Appendix D; § 42.12)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Testimony Guidelines appended to the Trial Practice Guide (Appendix D) apply to proceedings. The Board may impose sanctions for failure to adhere to the Testimony Guidelines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example sanction: reasonable expenses and attorneys’ fees incurred by any party may be levied on a person who impedes, delays, or frustrates fair examination of a witness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross-examination timing
rubrics_metrics.description: Cross-examination ordinarily takes place after any supplemental evidence is due (37 C.F.R. § 42.53(d)(2)) and ordinarily ends no later than one week before the filing date for any paper in which the cross-examination testimony is expected to be used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scheduling Order will set the precise dates; parties should coordinate with due dates for submitting papers that rely on cross-examination testimony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sample Scheduling Order — allowed filings and due dates (DUE DATE 1–7)
rubrics_metrics.description: A sample scheduling order sets specific due dates and identifies which filings are permitted on each due date. Highlights: DUE DATE 1 (3 months): Patent Owner response to petition and patent owner motion to amend (Patent Owner must confer with Board before filing motion to amend, request conference call no later than two weeks prior to DUE DATE 1). DUE DATE 2 (3 months): Petitioner’s reply to patent owner response; petitioner’s opposition to motion to amend. DUE DATE 3 (1 month): Patent Owner’s sur-reply to reply; Patent Owner’s reply to opposition to motion to amend. DUE DATE 4 (1 month): Petitioner’s sur-reply to reply to opposition to motion to amend; either party may file motion to exclude evidence (same as Due Date 4 but parties may not stipulate extension). DUE DATE 5 (~1 week): Opposition to motion to exclude. DUE DATE 6 (~1 week): Reply to opposition to motion to exclude; request for prehearing conference. DUE DATE 7 (~2 weeks): Oral argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parties may stipulate different dates for DUE DATES 1–5 (earlier or later, but no later than DUE DATE 6). Parties may not stipulate extensions of DUE DATES 6 and 7 or to requests for oral hearing. The Due Date Appendix provides a calendar view and the approximate intervals (months/weeks) for each due date.
